He moved through the shop like a dark cloud drifting across a summer sky, bringing with him a chill that had nothing to do with the weather, but everything to do with the impenetrable gloom that seemed to emanate from his very person. I felt, in those days, that Orlick was a man who lived entirely within himself, and that his self was a place where no light could ever hope to penetrate.

passage: The Constables and the Bow Street men from London—for, this happened in the days of the extinct red-waistcoated police—were about the house for a week or two, and did pretty much what I have heard and read of like authorities doing in other such cases. They took up several obviously wrong people, and they ran their heads very hard against wrong ideas, and persisted in trying to fit the circumstances to the ideas, instead of trying to extract ideas from the circumstances. Also, they stood about the door of the Jolly Bargemen, with knowing and reserved looks that filled the whole neighbourhood with admiration; and they had a mysterious manner of taking their drink, that was almost as good as taking the culprit. But not quite, for they never did it. Long after these constitutional powers had dispersed, my sister lay very ill in bed. Her sight was disturbed, so that she saw objects multiplied, and grasped at visionary teacups and wineglasses instead of the realities; her hearing was greatly impaired; her memory also; and her speech was unintelligible. When, at last, she came round so far as to be helped downstairs, it was still necessary to keep my slate always by her, that she might indicate in writing what she could not indicate in speech. As she was (very bad handwriting apart) a more than indifferent speller, and as Joe was a more than indifferent reader, extraordinary complications arose between them which I was always called in to solve. The administration of mutton instead of medicine, the substitution of

the substitution of coarse, unseasoned beef for the delicate restorative broths required by her constitution. It was a comedy of errors played out in the shadow of a tragedy. Joe, whose literacy was as stunted as his temperament was blunt, would approach her slate with the grim determination of a man attempting to decipher an ancient, cursed hieroglyph. He would squint at her scrawled, illegible characters, his brow furrowed in a way that suggested he was battling not just the letters, but the very concept of meaning itself.

I, the weary arbiter of this domestic chaos, found myself perpetually caught between his stubborn ignorance and her fractured perception. He would misinterpret a request for a simple compress as a demand for a heavy meal, or mistake a plea for silence for a command to fetch more ale. The tension in the room was a palpable, suffocating thing; the air was thick with the scent of medicinal herbs and the heavy, unwashed atmosphere of a man who understood the world only through the blunt force of his hands. Every failed communication was a miniature catastrophe, a reminder that in the struggle between a fading mind and a blunt soul, the truth was often the first casualty.

Joe, possessed of a reading ability that could be described as purely decorative, approached the written word with the same suspicion a cat might reserve for a wet sponge; he would squint at the slate, turn it upside down, and eventually conclude that a particularly jagged 'S' was actually a request for more salt. My sister, in her state of sensory confusion, would write instructions that were less a guide for recovery and more a series of cryptic riddles. She might intend to ask for water but, through a combination of failing sight and a wandering mind, would scrawl a demand for a new pair of boots. I found myself acting as a sort of linguistic diplomat, mediating between a man who could not decipher a menu and a woman who could no longer distinguish a spoon from a prayer. The tension of her illness was constantly punctuated by these absurdities, creating a domestic atmosphere where one never knew if the next crisis would be a medical emergency or a profound misunderstanding regarding the necessity of gravy.
